about: Fingerprints for dangling-resource takeover, read by `scripts/takeover`.
Every published takeover list is partly stale. Providers add domain
verification, change their unclaimed-host body, or retire a product, and the
lists keep the entry. So each entry here carries three separate facts instead
of one 'vulnerable' bit:
fingerprint  what the provider's own unclaimed-host response looks like.
This is the only part a black-box test observes directly.
claimable    whether registering that name is actually possible TODAY.
yes     the name is first-come and nothing else gates it.
edge    a claim is possible only sometimes: the provider asks
for domain verification, a paid plan, or a support
ticket, so a fingerprint match alone proves nothing.
no      the provider verifies domain ownership before it will
serve a custom domain, so the dangling record is a
hygiene problem and not a takeover.
unknown nobody here checked. Treated like `edge`.
confidence   how much this repository trusts the entry.
high    corroborated against first-party provider behaviour or
documentation, or a published incident.
medium  consistent across sources, provider side not re-checked.
low     carried over from a published list and NOT corroborated.
`stale: true` says so again in one word.
`scripts/takeover` writes `candidate` only for claimable=yes with
confidence>=medium. Everything else becomes `inconclusive`, with the reason.
It never writes `confirmed` (that word belongs to the validate phase) and it
never claims anything.
Re-checking an entry means reading the provider's current documentation and,
on an engagement, the live unclaimed-host response — not copying another list.
Set `checked` to the date when you do, and raise `confidence`.

body_any: The specified bucket does not exist

services.claim_path: CreateBucket with the exact bucket name in the exact region, then a static-website or CloudFront origin. Bucket names are unique per AWS partition, so the first account to ask gets it.
services.note: The strongest and oldest case. A virtual-hosted URL carries the bucket name in the host, so the dangling name IS the bucket name.
services.source: AWS S3 bucket naming rules (globally unique per partition) + can-i-take-over-xyz

body_any: The specified bucket does not exist

services.claim_path: Create a bucket with that name in any project. GCS bucket names are globally unique. Google does require domain verification for a bucket whose NAME is a domain (`www.example.com`), which is a separate case from a CNAME to `c.storage.googleapis.com` fronting an arbitrary bucket name.
services.note: Read the dangling reference carefully: `bucket.storage.googleapis.com` and `storage.googleapis.com/bucket` carry the bucket name in different places.
services.source: Google Cloud Storage bucket naming + domain-named bucket verification docs

body_any: The specified account does not exist

services.claim_path: Create a storage account with the same account name in any subscription; account names are globally unique in `*.blob.core.windows.net`.
services.note: Deleted storage accounts free their name immediately, which is what makes this live.
services.source: Azure storage account naming (globally unique) + can-i-take-over-xyz

services.claim_path: Create a Traffic Manager profile with the same DNS prefix. Profile names are globally unique in `trafficmanager.net`, and a deleted profile's name is reusable.
services.note: There is no HTTP fingerprint: a deleted profile's name is simply NXDOMAIN. That makes it a DNS-only judgement and a clean one.
services.source: Azure Traffic Manager profile naming + can-i-take-over-xyz

services.claim_path: Create an App Service / CDN endpoint with the same name, then add the custom domain. Azure asks for a domain-verification TXT record (`asuid.<host>`) for a custom domain on App Service, so a bare CNAME is not always enough.
services.note: NXDOMAIN on the `*.azurewebsites.net` target is the signal. Whether the claim then completes depends on which Azure product and whether `asuid` verification applies.
services.source: Azure custom-domain verification (asuid TXT) docs + can-i-take-over-xyz

body_any: There isn't a GitHub Pages site here.
For root URLs (like http://example.com/) you must provide an index.html file

services.claim_path: Create a repository, enable Pages, add the dangling host as the Pages custom domain. GitHub introduced custom-domain verification for organizations: a verified domain cannot be taken by another account, so the claim succeeds only when the original owner never verified it.
services.note: Fingerprint is reliable and easy to read; CLAIMABILITY is the uncertain half. Report the fingerprint, state the verification question, let the operator decide.
services.source: GitHub docs: verifying a custom domain for GitHub Pages (verification added 2022) + can-i-take-over-xyz

services.claim_path: Create an app and add the dangling host as a custom domain. Heroku refuses a domain already attached to another app, so this works only once the original app or domain entry is gone.
services.note: Heroku's free tier ended in 2022 and a lot of dangling herokuapp CNAMEs date from that; the fingerprint is common, the claim is not always open.

services.claim_path: Create a site and add the custom domain. Netlify asks for verification when a domain is already registered to another team, so the outcome depends on whether the original team removed it.
services.note: The body contains a request id, so match on the prefix, not the whole string.

body_any: The deployment could not be found

services.claim_path: Not open: Vercel requires the domain to be verified (a TXT record, or the domain added to the account) before it serves it, so adding somebody else's dangling host to your own project does not work.
services.note: A dangling Vercel CNAME is still worth reporting as DNS hygiene and as a phishing-adjacent dead reference, but it is not a takeover. `scripts/takeover` reports it as not-dangling-but-dead, never as a candidate.
services.source: Vercel custom-domain verification docs + can-i-take-over-xyz (not vulnerable)

body_any: Please check that this domain has been added to a service

services.claim_path: Add the domain to a Fastly service on your own account. Fastly has historically allowed this; it needs a paid service and Fastly has added checks, so treat the fingerprint as a lead.
services.note: The 'unknown domain' page is unambiguous about the state and says nothing about whether a claim is open.

body_any: Sorry, this shop is currently unavailable
To learn more about this store

services.claim_path: Add the domain to your own store. Shopify asks for domain verification and refuses a domain connected elsewhere, so the claim is conditional.
services.note: Three different bodies appear depending on the store's state; only 'currently unavailable' means the store is gone.

services.claim_path: Create an environment with the same CNAME prefix in the same region. Beanstalk environment CNAMEs are unique per region, and AWS added a random suffix to new environment URLs, so an old short name is claimable and a suffixed one is not.
services.note: An `*.elb.amazonaws.com` target is an ELB hostname, not a claimable name: that is an A/alias case, not a takeover.
services.source: AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment CNAME docs + can-i-take-over-xyz

body_any: The page you have requested does not exist

services.claim_path: Create a repository named after the host and enable the static-site feature. NOT corroborated here: Bitbucket's static-site hosting has changed, and the entry may no longer exist as a product.
services.note: Carried from published lists and not re-checked. A match is inconclusive until somebody reads Bitbucket's current docs.
